title: What does Houthi advance mean for Yemen’s southern separatists?
author: Adam Lucente
text:
Analysis

What does Houthi advance mean for Yemen’s southern separatists?

The Southern Transitional Council remains somewhat active in southern Yemen after its territorial defeat by the Saudi-backed government, and the Houthis are not interested in fighting the group at present.

Adam Lucente

Sep 12, 2026

Yemen’s southern separatists said they are still willing to cooperate with the Saudi-backed government in the fight against the Houthis after the Iran-backed group made sweeping gains in the south and west. One Yemeni expert said that the anti-Houthi coalition has been severely weakened by the tensions between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates over south Yemen, making a counteroffensive difficult. The Houthis captured Mayyun Island on Friday, giving them control of the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait area along the Red Sea. They seized the Red Sea port city of Mokha on Thursday, following an offensive in the western Taiz province that began last week. 'Political and military failure'Ambassador Khaled Alyemany, a US-based adviser to the Southern Transitional Council presidency, said the Houthi gains are “not a surprise and a result of accumulated political and military failure.” “The Houthis were left unattended until they received instructions from Tehran to take Bab al-Mandeb,” Alyemany, a former Yemeni foreign minister, told Al-Monitor.  “The next step is closing it and using the same tactics as in Hormuz.” The Southern Transitional Council formed in 2017 and supports self-determination for southern Yemen, which was independent from 1967 to 1990. The STC and its armed wing, known as the Security Belt Forces, were backed by the UAE. The STC was nominally a part of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government’s coalition against the Houthis, but launched an offensive against government forces in December 2025, capturing large swaths of the south. Backed by Saudi air power, government forces launched a counter-offensive, and by mid-January, the gains had been reversed. The UAE said in late December it would withdraw its forces in Yemen. The crisis was largely the result of rising tensions between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh. The UAE's support for southern separatism contrasted with the Saudi effort to reach a peace deal with the Houthis, Al-Monitor reported at the time. Both countries are seeking regional influence and also diverge on Sudan and Somalia. The UAE has economic interests in the breakaway state Somaliland and allegedly supports the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan, though Abu Dhabi denies this. Saudi Arabia is close to the Sudanese armed forces and the Somali government. Members of the STC announced the group’s dissolution from Riyadh in January, though other council members have rejected this and figures associated with the body say it remains active.Alyemany said that the STC had expressed a desire to help counter the Houthis in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, but said the Saudi-backed coalition “sees the STC as an enemy.” He said the council is still “willing” to work with Yemeni and international forces in the country to cooperate against the Houthis. “American leadership should bring all components together,” said Alyemany, appealing to the Trump administration. The Yemeni government’s armed forces said later on Friday that they had begun striking Houthi positions in southwest Yemen, including near Mokha. The Yemen Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to Al-Monitor’s request for comment. A divided southMohammed al-Basha, founder of the US-based risk advisory Basha Report, said that the STC’s main base of power is the southwest Al-Dhale province, north of Aden, adding that it retains a presence in Aden, Hadhramaut and other parts of the south as well. “Whatever remaining force they have is in the low thousands,” Basha told Al-Monitor. “But they’re still obviously on the ground.”Former STC leader Aidarus al-Zubaidi is currently in exile in the UAE, and a number of other members have resigned or joined other armed groups. Basha said the STC views the Houthis as “northerners and foreigners,” and said the council remains in a “defensive posture” against the Iranian proxy.“Before the UAE-Saudi breakup, the STC would’ve joined forces with northern forces to expel Houthis from certain locations, but we won’t see that today,” he said, though he added that the southern Yemenis will “defend their territory” if attacked. “The UAE-Saudi spat weakened the anti-Houthi coalition from the core,” he added. Basha described the Houthis as being “very careful” in dealing with the south, noting that the Houthis have not yet moved into the southwestern tip of Yemen that was part of former South Yemen. “They’ve issued statements saying they are not trying to occupy the south. They’re probably trying to pressure the south into a (new) structure,” he said. Basha said the Houthi reluctance to move on parts of the south is practical. “They know they have no base of support in the south. They know it’s going to be a tough battle and they can’t kill their way through the whole country,” he said. “But I think eventually if they don’t get what they want, they will push ahead.” A Houthi spokesperson did not immediately respond to Al-Monitor’s request for comment. Various armed groups in the south are partaking in the fight with the Houthis. The Washington-based Institute for the Study of War identified the National Shield Forces, the Southern Giants Brigades and the National Resistance Forces as the main targets of the Houthi offensive in the southwest Taiz province, as well as Hadhramaut further north.The National Shield Forces were formed by the government’s Presidential Leadership Council. The National Resistance Forces are led by Tareq Saleh, nephew of the late former President Ali Abdullah Saleh, and fight alongside the government. The Southern Giants Brigades were previously backed by the UAE but now cooperate with the government as well.One southern Yemeni source familiar with the situation said that the STC is divided on how to handle the Houthi advance, with some members working on social media to deter action against them out of anger toward Saudi Arabia. “Other STC members…view any Houthi advance toward the south or the western coastline of Yemen as an existential threat,” said the source. “Politically, they see these advances as definitive proof that northern-dominated government forces are infiltrated by Houthi operatives and cannot hold territory.”
